story_type: sinking exercise filmed by cameras aboard the target ship
hook: Engineers bolted cameras to this warship. Then the missiles hit.
narration: These cameras were bolted to a warship so they could film the missiles hitting it.
The ship was the retired frigate Klakring, sent to a range off the coast of Scotland.
For about a year and a half, Navy engineers wired her with sensors, cables and power.
Once the live fire began, nobody could go back aboard.
The destroyer Paul Ignatius fired a Standard Missile 6 built to strike ships.
The Royal Navy fired its newest ship-busting missiles, the Naval Strike Missile and Sea Venom.
[short pause] Every hit was data. Sensors aboard measured the damage, so the Navy learns how real ships fail and what they need to be repaired.
Between strikes, engineers ran stability software to judge whether she could take the next one.
Fragments tore up the sea all along her side.
outcome: Then the submarine USS Massachusetts fired a Mark 48 torpedo, the final hit, and the Klakring sank.
title: Cameras on a warship as missiles hit
description:
Cameras aboard the decommissioned frigate ex-USS Klakring film missile strikes during Exercise Atlantic Thunder 2026, a U.S. and U.K. sinking exercise in the North Atlantic off Scotland in September 2026.

Footage: U.S. Navy video by Mass Communication Specialist 1st Class Austin Ingram, via DVIDS: https://www.dvidshub.net/video/1024853/atlantic-thunder-26-b-roll

extra_sources.excerpt: During the SINKEX, the guided-missile destroyer USS Paul Ignatius (DDG 117) successfully demonstrated maximum damage and range capability of an anti-surface variant of the Standard Missile 6 (SM 6). USS Massachusetts (SSN 798) successfully engaged the target with the Mk 48 Advanced Capability Torpedo, resulting in the final hit and ultimately sinking ex-USS Klakring. During the exercise, the Royal Navy confirmed its newest ship-busting missiles, the Naval Strike Missile (NSM) and Sea Venom.

Prior to the start of the exercise Naval Surface Warfare Center Carderock and Naval Information Warfare Center (NIWC) Pacific used sensors placed on the target ship to perform battle damage assessments. The data gathered will be used in post-exercise damage assessments to provide critical information to rapidly identify system failures, determine repair needs, and strengthen the Navy’s future real-world response.

The U.S.-U.K. multi-domain sinking exercise , conducted off the coast of Scotland and led by U.S. 6th Fleet, brought together participating forces for live-fire engagements against the former Navy ship.

For roughly a year and a half, Carderock engineers worked to prepare Klakring as an instrumented target. They installed sensors, ran cables, prepared power systems and developed ways to collect information remotely. Once the live-fire events began, personnel could not return aboard to inspect the damage, adjust equipment or retrieve what they had installed.

Using weapons-effects and stability prediction software, engineers assessed Klakring's condition as the exercise progressed. Hulk status reports summarized their findings, providing the mission director and participating units with updates on the target ship's condition and informing decisions about whether it was ready for subsequent events.
